articles.title_orig: North Korea - Building an Alliance with China and Russia
articles.title_zh: North Korea - Building an Alliance with China and Russia
articles.content_orig:
Propaganda, military posturing and a nuclear program are shoring up Kim Jong Un's power, both domestically and internationally.
This documentary traces North Korea' s evolution from an isolated hereditary dictatorship to a state whose nuclear weapons program is cause for global concern. Today, the regime possesses missiles capable of potentially reaching long-range targets. Meanwhile, it is also seeking closer ties with key partners China and Russia . And for the first time, North Korea is deploying thousands of soldiers to fight alongside Russia in its war in Ukraine — a conspicuous move that provides the country combat experience, foreign currency, and access to new military technology.
Drawing on new archival sources, exclusive analysis from experts and insights into North Korea's elaborate propaganda machine, this documentary shows how the regime fosters loyalty and cements its power. A cult of personality, shows of military strength and foreign policy successes all serve to maintain its power at home.
This underscores why Kim Jong Un currently sees himself in a strategically advantageous position — and why Pyongyang's role on the international stage is becoming increasingly significant.
Despite being a small, largely isolated country, North Korea regularly finds itself at the center of geopolitical tensions. Three generations of the Kim dynasty have created a system of government based on control, isolation and military strength. What strategies have allowed the Kim family to continue ruling to this day — and what are the consequences for the region and the world?

articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia seeks to pressure China over Houthi arms without risking ties

Similar withdrawals from UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain reported as concerns grow about restart of war on Iran after US midterm elections
The US state department has ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia as the gulf kingdom faces a barrage of near-daily attacks, with at least three people killed at an airport and oilfield.
Attacks on “civilian airports and other critical infrastructure” by the Iranian-supported Houthis in Yemen were highlighted as the reason for the drawdown. The state department spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said: “The safety and security of department personnel and their families remain our highest priority.”
The state department said the order covered its embassy in Riyadh and its satellite consulates. The embassy had been badly damaged at the start of the US war on Iran and had been operating with only a skeleton staff for months, although in recent weeks some diplomats had returned.
Media outlets – including NBC and AFP – reported that families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn from the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, while the New York Times said the Trump administration was developing plans to restart the war on Iran.
However, in his statement on Wednesday, Pigott described the reports of further withdrawals as “inaccurate” and said the state department order was for the departure of staff and their families from Saudi Arabia only.
Saudi Arabia has faced a succession of deadly attacks from the Houthis over recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport which was the kingdom’s deadliest in years as the war with the group escalates.
On Thursday the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority announced that two people had been killed in overnight attacks on King Fahd international airport in Dammam on the Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.
Eight people were injured and there was material damage to the airport, according to officials. The global flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said flights had been diverted away from the airport.
Separately, falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility in the country’s south-east killed two people and injured a further two, the Saudi energy ministry said.
The Houthis said on Thursday ⁠they ⁠had ​launched attacks on ⁠Saudi Arabia’s defence ministry in ⁠Riyadh, Saudi ​Aramco ‌facilities ‌in Yanbu ‌and King Fahd international airport in Dammam.
Essential workers at Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in the east of the country were told to evacuate on Thursday, two sources told Agence France-Presse, after their non-essential colleagues were told to work from home since last week.
The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf in late February before the start of its war against Iran. NBC reported that the US military had been quietly scaling back its presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, but a spokesperson from US central command told the US news outlet that service members were regularly moved to “optimize mission readiness”.
The withdrawal of staff from the region coincides with reports that Trump has been presented with plans for restarting strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.
The New York Times reported that the US and Israel had developed plans for a “short but intensive operation” after the defense secretary, Peter Hegseth, travelled to Israel earlier this week for meetings with the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
Last week ⁠Trump said the US was hoping to knock out Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain , a site linked to the country’s ⁠nuclear program, however the US president has publicly said he does not intend to restart the war before the 3 November elections.

articles.title_orig: Airbnb guests freed from chores involving ‘significant effort’ under new global rules
articles.title_zh: Airbnb guests freed from chores involving ‘significant effort’ under new global rules
articles.content_orig:
Washing and putting away dishes are examples of chores that Airbnb says guests should generally not be asked to do
Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.
The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.
Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.
The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace.
"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC.
"So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."
According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".
The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.
A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and  will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.
Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.
While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.
If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree.
Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees.
TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail.
One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place.
They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted
Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts.

articles.title_zh: Is it safe to go to China right now? What the U.S. State Department travel advisory warns about wrongful detentions
articles.content_orig:
Ben is based in South Africa and also works on The Telegraph's Global Health Security team. He spent five years in Kabul covering the Afghanistan war, five years as Defence Correspondent in London, and four years in Islamabad
The United States has urged citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya, raising its travel alert level after the country reported an eighth case of Ebola.
The East African nation has recorded a rash of cases linked to a Kenyan businessman who died after travelling from Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
DRC is currently enduring the second worst Ebola outbreak on record with more than 4,000 deaths since May, though the true toll is thought to be far higher.
“The level was changed from Level 2 to Level 3 due to health risks,” the US embassy in Kenya said, a day after the State Department issued renewed travel advice for its citizens.
“Reconsider travel in Kenya due to risk of health, crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and traffic safety. Some areas have increased risk,” it said.
The alert came as Kenyan doctors leaders demanded better protective equipment against the highly infectious virus.
Three of the confirmed Ebola cases are reported to be health staff who cared for the businessman and the others are thought to be relatives who visited him.
Health unions have said staff should not be forced to put their lives at risk because of inadequate protective gear and have also raised concerns of short-staffing and a lack of preparedness in hospitals.
The Ebola virus is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood and saliva, and health workers or close relatives tending to the sick are particularly prone to getting infected themselves.
Dr Ibrahim Matende, president of the Kenya Medical Association, said: “Every healthcare worker deserves a safe working environment and timely access to the highest standard of care.”
The cases in Kenya have also raised questions about biosecurity and surveillance in the region after the index case – a Kenyan national living in eastern DRC – took flights and crossed international borders despite apparently becoming increasingly ill and showing Ebola-like symptoms.
The businessman had been unwell for two weeks when on October 1 he boarded a domestic flight from Kisangani to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has in recent weeks become one of the outbreak’s main hotspots.
Crossing over into Uganda, he then travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on October 3. Uganda has not reported any cases so far.
A relative collected him and drove him to the private Nairobi Hospital, while he was suffering with fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
He was confirmed to be infected with the Bundibugyo strain of the virus and died two days later.
Meanwhile, Africa’s top public health agency and Congolese officials have raised concerns that over $700 million in Ebola aid is unaccounted for, and called on aid groups to provide more information about their finances, Associated Press reported.
Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said last week that international donors had transferred close to a billion dollars to aid organisations in eastern DRC since the outbreak was declared in mid-May.
But only $200 million has been accounted for by international and local organisations working on the ground.
Only one-third of the organisations attended a recent meeting organised by Congo’s health ministry and provided their financial records, Dr Kaseya said.
Those attending said they received $228 million, of which $127 ⁠million had been spent and around $100 million remained available.
Dr Kaseya did not identify which organisations had not provided their records.
“This represents a significant lack of transparency and financial reporting on the part of these organisations, preventing the Government from having a comprehensive overview of the resources mobilised, how they were utilised and the results achieved,” the Africa CDC said.
“It is unacceptable for organisations to receive hundreds of millions of dollars to intervene in a country facing a major health emergency without providing a transparent account to the national authorities responsible for coordinating the response.

articles.title_orig: Jobless claims near the lowest since the 1960s as low-fire trend continues
articles.title_zh: Jobless claims near the lowest since the 1960s as low-fire trend continues
articles.content_orig:
Employers continue to hold onto workers even as hiring remains weak, sending weekly jobless claims to around their lowest levels in records that stretch back nearly six decades.
Initial filings for unemployment insurance slipped to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ending Oct. 17, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
That marked another leg lower in the low-fire trend, with the total just off the 189,000 reported for the week of July 18 that was the lowest since September 1969. Claims have averaged 212,000 over the past year, and the four-week moving average is down to 197,750.
Those numbers come against an uncertain backdrop for the labor market.
Nonfarm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September and have averaged a gain of just 69,000 a month in 2026. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, an increase largely due to a sharp spike in labor force participation. Layoffs have remained modest, declining by 61,000 in August, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Sept. 29.
Over the prior 12 months, the layoff rate measured as a share of the total workforce fell to 1%, down 0.2 percentage point during the period. Job openings were relatively flat during the period.
"Despite extremely pessimistic views expressed in consumer confidence surveys regarding the economy overall, countless headlines describing job cuts from a variety of businesses, and the phantom job-stealing power of AI, the claims data suggests that labor market conditions are stable," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a client note.
The data comes during the reference week that the BLS uses to calculate the payrolls growth number. The September jobs report will be released Nov. 5.
Federal Reserve officials gather next week to issue their latest decision on interest rates . Policymakers in recent days have characterized the labor market as a source of general strength and focused more of their attention on the nettlesome inflation problem that has kept the pace of price increases well above the central bank's 2% target.
Markets expect the Fed to hold off on a rate hike in October but then to institute another quarter percentage point increase in December.

articles.title_orig: French weekend protests to be limited to union demos only, says Macron
articles.title_zh: French weekend protests to be limited to union demos only, says Macron
articles.content_orig:
Only authorised union protests will be allowed in French towns and cities on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron has said, after demonstrations across the country turned violent last weekend.
Speaking as some cities including Lyon and Nice imposed complete bans, Macron said "illegitimate" protests would not be allowed but unions would be offered alternative routes so that businesses could be protected.
Big demonstrations against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed last Saturday by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed.
Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said law enforcement would be 20% higher than it was last weekend, after the government had promised a "massive" police deployment.
At least 2,500 people have been arrested across France since the disorder broke out and Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday.
"The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."
He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic".
Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.
The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.
In Lyon, France's third-biggest city, regional authorities have imposed a blanket ban on demonstrations.
"In light of the mobilisation that is circulating and in view of the events of 17 October, the prefect has decided to prohibit by decree any demonstration in the city of Lyon this Saturday," the Rhône prefecture said in a statement.
Similar announcements have been made in Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.
Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.
Around 550,000 thousand people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests .
Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.
Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests.
Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the office, housed in a 19th-Century building, was "a tragedy".
In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started.
The iconic Place de la République was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc.
Following the unrest, France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez tendered his resignation, which was rejected by President Macron.
The Élysée Palace asked him instead to look at how to make France's streets safer and bring rioters to justice.
Nuñez said his teams had forecast 200,000 demonstrators, a figure much lower than the 550,000 estimated to have gathered.
The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

Associate Editor & YouTube Host
As a longtime user of the original, Neil was excited to see what the new COROS DURA 2 SOLAR had in store. His review dives into his impressions of the new head unit, how it differs from the much-beloved debut model, and whether the price jump is worth it for those considering the upgrade. Find his full video and written reviews below…
Additional photos by Logan Watts
Today, we’re looking at a new head unit, the COROS DURA 2 SOLAR. It looks unlike any I’ve ever seen. In my latest review, I’ll be diving into the details you need to know, including the specs, some interesting new features, a few major head-scratchers, and my first impressions. Check out my full video review followed by a written version below.
The original DURA was, and still is, an amazing head unit. It has the best battery life of any head unit I’ve ever used, a simple interface in a sea of increasingly complicated options, and, best of all, a very affordable $250 price tag. COROS made a splash in the cycling world, and the DURA became one of the best head units for bikepacking. In fact, I’ll say it: for trips longer than three days, it’s my first choice because of its battery life. Before the first DURA release, COROS wasn’t exactly a household name in cycling. Despite its success, it still might not be a household name. But it gained plenty of recognition for delivering a head unit that lasts a ridiculously long time without breaking the bank, giving it a solid foothold in a saturated industry.
That said, COROS released the first DURA before it was truly ready. Maybe that’s why the price tag was so enticing. Did it get the job done? Yes. But as I mentioned in my *original review*, there were some hiccups. I held off on reviewing it until a few firmware updates had addressed enough of those issues. Doing a first look at the DURA 2 SOLAR hurts a little, because I know I haven’t put it through the kind of testing I normally would for a full review. But most of those early growing pains seem to be behind us. And during my initial testing, the DURA 2 has felt much more refined and ready for market. And yes, it’s pretty darn weird-looking.
The unit comes in a nice box. Open it up, and you’ll find the DURA 2 SOLAR with stickers identifying the dials and buttons. It also comes with a lanyard to wrap around the bars or stem for security, which I always use with head units. I appreciate that COROS still includes what looks like a quality, long USB-C to USB-C cable and a bunch of instructions. Oddly enough, my test unit didn’t come with a mount. Logan got the new aluminum one, and he said it’s well-made and sleek, and it comes with a GoPro-style undermount option for lights or a camera.
Since plenty of customers already have mounts, you can buy the unit on its own or pay extra for a version with a mount. I asked COROS to send me one, but it didn’t arrive in time. Packaging isn’t a major factor in the overall experience of any piece of tech, but it’s well done here: clean, nearly all recyclable, and thoughtfully put together. Many cycling head unit companies have dialed that in over the last few years, and I appreciate it.
The DURA 2 SOLAR is a big departure from the original unit. The original unit positioned itself as a budget option amid increasingly expensive computers. I don’t know if this was the plan all along, but bringing an affordable head unit into a market with so few budget options made a lot of sense. Add the incredible battery life, and the original DURA was a unicorn. But breaking into the cycling industry as a relatively unknown brand isn’t easy. COROS mentioned that DURA sales were a little slow at first, but picked up as more people learned about the price and user feedback and reviews started rolling in.
Instead of updating the DURA and maintaining that price point, COROS decided to go premium. I’ll admit it’s a little disappointing, especially since they’re discontinuing the original. I’m sad to see that option go, and it feels like a massive miss. Let’s hope they bring a lower-budget option to the table, but I’m not holding my breath. If anything, I think they might drop “SOLAR” from the product name and launch a non-solar unit at a slightly lower price, but that would eliminate one of the new unit’s best features.
I’ve always thought of COROS as a brand for the people. I’ve used their watches for three years now, and between the features, battery life, and price, they’re pretty hard to beat. It gave me the impression that a brand could build good products, deliver a strong user experience, and still make a profit without charging top dollar. That said, the DURA 2 SOLAR comes in at $499 without a mount or $549 with one. That puts the unit alone at roughly twice the price of the first DURA, which launched just two years ago. Inflation aside, that’s a pretty big jump. So, let’s dive into the differences and see whether the new one is worth it.
The new DURA 2 SOLAR is a looker. It uses a carbon-and-alloy construction, compared to the first DURA’s mostly plastic body, and they weigh about the same: 100 grams for the DURA 2 SOLAR and 101 grams for the other. The overall shape is strange. It almost looks like a concept car, and COROS seems to be leaning into aerodynamics. The upper portion is only 5.7mm thick, easily the thinnest of any head unit I’ve tested. It thickens toward the main body near the quarter-turn mount. It’s similar in width to the original but significantly longer, measuring 117mm long, 58mm wide, and 17mm thick. Overall, it feels nice in the hand and is fairly lightweight. Once you attach it to the quarter-turn mount, it sits nicely out front. From the top, it doesn’t look nearly as ridiculous as it does from the side.
The controls have changed too. It has two physical buttons, one on each side, but the oversized watch-style scroll dial is gone, which I really enjoyed using. Now you get two haptic buttons at the bottom, plus an updated touchscreen that feels much more sensitive and responsive than the original. You can also charge the device using the USB-C port below the right button. The larger 3.5” display is a welcome change. This was one of my complaints with the original, especially when navigating: it seemed like they could have fit a larger screen into the body. I think they’ve done a good job addressing that here. In my initial testing, the touchscreen works well, and I like the haptic feedback. And paired with the side buttons, it’s intuitive and relatively simple to use.
Speaking of the screen, the DURA 2 SOLAR still uses a sunlight-readable, Memory-in-Pixel, or MIP, display designed for low power consumption. Howeve

Marvel's Wolverine led US game sales in September, achieving the highest monthly dollar sales for a Sony-published title since Helldivers 2.
Sony continued its hardware momentum, with PlayStation 5 leading both unit and dollar sales according to Circana data.
PS5 spending rose 43% year over year, and unit sales increased 22%, resulting in Sony's highest monthly hardware dollar share since May 2025.
Overall hardware spending rose 12% to $362 million in September, offsetting declines in dollar sales for Nintendo Switch 2 (down 12%) and Xbox Series X|S (down 2%).
Xbox Series X|S unit sales declined 27% in the US last month, with Xbox Ecosystem console sales reaching a record September low. Switch 2 unit sales decreased 14%.
Total content spending dropped 2% to $4.2 billion in September, led by a 14% decline in mobile. Console spending grew 8%, and PC spending rose 27%.
Eight new games debuted on the US chart in September. Marvel's Wolverine moved NBA 2K27 to No. 2 and outperformed EA Sports FC 27.
Despite its drop, NBA 2K27 surpassed Resident Evil Requiem to become the best-selling game of 2026 year-to-date.
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave and Blood of the Dawnwalker completed the Top 5. Other new September entries included Wardogs, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Halloween: The Game, and Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

Sony is seemingly exiting the UHD Blu-ray player market, as it ends shipments of its UBP-X700/K device with no replacement in sight.
If accurate, it means Panasonic is the only recognisable consumer electronics manufacturer still making UHD Blu-ray players, although some Chinese companies are beginning to fill the void.
While the Japanese giant has not issued a press release on this topic, blog – and official Sony retailer – Kunkoku reports that the company has ceased shipping the abovementioned product.

This is reflected on the company’s own website , where the UBP-X700/K is currently listed as out of stock with no plans to ship new units in the future.
Technically the PS5 is a UHD Blu-ray player as well, although the platform holder has obviously signalled its intent to stop shipping disc-based games in January 2028 . It’s unlikely the PS6 will come with a disc drive.
None of this should come as a surprise, by the way – Sony has been shedding many of its consumer electronics products , as it transitions more towards entertainment.
The market for standalone UHD Blu-ray players in 2026 is also likely to be vanishingly small.
If you want one of these, it does look like there are still units available in Europe and the US, but you may need to act fast as it doesn’t look like these will be restocked.
It’s possible Sony may announce a replacement product in the future, but looking at the way things are going, I wouldn’t hold my breath.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX and Tesla Are Already Joined at the Hip. What a Formal Merger Would Mean.
articles.title_zh: SpaceX and Tesla Are Already Joined at the Hip. What a Formal Merger Would Mean.
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX shares shot up more than 8% Wednesday morning after a better-than-expected earnings report and CEO Elon Musk’s revelation that SpaceX and Tesla had formed special committees to discuss a potential merger.
Asked about the long-rumored tie-up on an earnings call Tuesday, Musk voiced support for the idea while emphasizing that any deal would be decided by shareholders. “This is definitely kind of a question where I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield… but I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies.”
He added that a merger would be “a good idea,” and that “there’s a lot to be gained” from the two companies cooperating on AI software development, chip design and robotics.
As a “conflicted party,” Musk said, he cannot be a part of the committee discussions. Historically, Tesla shareholders have broadly fallen in line with Musk’s wishes, however.
The comments appeared to be the most forceful Musk has made publicly. When asked about a potential deal following SpaceX’s blockbuster July IPO, Musk didn’t offer an opinion one way or another, saying “obviously… we can’t talk about combining companies and that kind of thing on an earnings call. It’s got to be done with the appropriate process.”
Tesla shares rose more than 2% Wednesday morning.
Investors were also cheering SpaceX’s better-than-expected earnings report. The rocket, satellite internet and AI company brought in net income of $4.4 billion in the most recent quarter, swinging to a profit after back-to-back quarters of losses this year.
In its second earnings report since going public, SpaceX said it brought in $14.6 billion — up 161% year-over-year, according to the company, driven by what it called its “Super Intelligence” segment and its Starlink satellite-internet business.
The big questions about who’s to blame for Starshield disruptions in Ukraine
Wall Street analysts surveyed by FactSet had expected net income of $1.57 billion, with revenue of $12.9 billion. SpaceX reported earnings per share of 35 cents Tuesday, versus 14 cents forecast by analysts.
Moments before the earnings call Tuesday, the Wall Street Journal published a report saying that Musk “ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink” that blindsided Ukrainian officials.
Musk during the call did not address the Journal report, which cited unnamed people familiar with the matter. CNN couldn’t immediately verify the veracity of the report.
SpaceX didn’t immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment.
Ukraine accused SpaceX last week of severely hindering its defense by suddenly limiting its Starlink internet service, which uses satellites in low orbit. Ukraine has used Starlink and a related military-grade service, Starshield , to communicate quickly and to both launch and prevent drone attacks.
While Musk repeatedly suggested the White House was to blame for the disruption, the Trump administration has denied responsibility. On X, Musk emphasized that Starshield was “owned and controlled by the US government” and that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Meta ( META ) has created a new overhang on its stock that Wall Street wasn't expecting when it established a new class of stock.
The Street's advice to Mark Zuckerberg and his team: Issue the stock fast so the focus can return to the clear product momentum the company is enjoying with its new Muse AI agent .
"The sooner the better in our view as it would remove the overhang and the Street now knows it will have non-voting shares in Jan'27, and Meta can still do a substantial equity raise before then without even coming close to impacting Mark's voting control," JPMorgan analyst Doug Anmuth said.
Meta announced late Wednesday that it is establishing a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock, which effectively serves as a 2-for-1 stock split.
Under the scheme — in part designed to keep founder Mark Zuckerberg working in California as the 5% billionaire's tax looms — existing shareholders will receive one new nonvoting Class C share for every Class A or Class B share they hold. Trading is slated to begin in January 2027.
Issuing nonvoting stock allows Zuckerberg to raise external capital for Meta's AI build-out without diluting his personal voting control over the tech giant.
The news took some air out of the balloon on what was an impressive quarter for Meta amid signs that its AI investments are paying off.
Meta's core advertising business reported a 26% increase in total revenue to $64.6 billion, powered by AI-driven recommendations, higher ad volume, and rising ad prices.
GAAP earnings per share came in at $3.83 versus analyst estimates of $3.56.
Meta stock fell 2% in premarket trading on Thursday.
"Net/net, some near-term noise in Meta shares, but we're encouraged by core Advertising and Meta's outlook for strong overall revenue growth in 2027, and the path to superintelligence is increasingly clear w/the Muse series of models & products," Anmuth said.

A majority of Americans view artificial intelligence as a threat to broader society, even as half believe the technology delivers personal benefits to their daily lives, according to a nationwide ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll released Wednesday.
The poll revealed 57% of adults say AI is bad for society overall, compared to 42% who see it as a societal good.
A majority of Republicans (57%) say AI is personally good for them while a similar majority of Democrats say it's personally bad for them (55%), marking a contrast between the majority political parties before the midterms.
The survey reveals key partisan and generational divides over tech adoption. While 63% of Democrats and 58% of independents view AI's societal impact negatively, Republicans lean more favorable, with 51% calling it beneficial overall.
Anti-progressive anxiety remains centered on widespread job displacement, cybersecurity risks, and economic inequality, alongside broad opposition to the local expansion of energy-intensive AI data centers powering the underlying infrastructure.
Anthropic is pressing forward with plans for a mid-November initial public offering (IPO), standing as the sole major AI firm remaining on a fall tech calendar otherwise emptied by rising interest rates and market volatility.
The AI lab is expected to make its prospectus public as early as late October and begin marketing shares to prospective investors during the week of Nov. 9.
Anthropic's listing will test whether its central role in the AI sector – where it is eyeing a valuation of up to $1.5 trillion – can overcome broader market headwinds.
Rising interest rates and growing skepticism around massive data center expenditures have forced peers to pull or delay their listings.
CoreWeave has suffered a steep selloff in shares and bonds, while infrastructure providers including Switch, Nscale, SB Energy, Elice, AirTrunk REIT, and Firmus have all paused or postponed their public offerings.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Kansas Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton admitted during a debate that he is "not sure" which specific federal AI regulations he would back, even as he urged lawmakers to establish an oversight agency modeled after the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
"The reason why I'm not sure is because I don't think anybody in Congress really fully understands the dangers of AI ," Hamilton, a pastor and founder of the Church of the Resurrection in Leawood, argued.
Leaving AI oversight to tech companies is a "bad idea," he added, calling on Congress to enlist industry experts to prevent threats to future generations.
Incumbent opponent Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., advocated for a "light touch" regulatory approach focused on national security, domestic privacy, and staying ahead of China.
Marshall pushed back against broad global regulatory frameworks, warning that adversarial nations like Russia and China would never abide by international rules that Democrats and globalists push.
The U.S. Commerce Department announced plans Thursday to award $389 million in research and development funding to four tech companies advancing power semiconductor devices and critical materials.
Under the agreement, the federal government will receive minority, non-controlling equity stakes in exchange for the capital injection.
Drawn from a $10 billion R&D fund established by Congress in 2022 , the awards target next-generation chip technology for fusion power, AI hardware, and raw material purification.
Helion will receive up to $175 million for fusion-generator semiconductors, while Commonwealth Fusion Systems is slated for up to $85 million. Additionally, Vertical Semiconductor will obtain up to $73 million to advance gallium nitride chips for AI data centers, and Sibelco will receive up to $56 million for ultra-high-purity quartz processing.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Spotify Co-CEO Gustav Söderström pushed back against claims that third-party AI agents will disrupt music streaming interfaces, asserting that user listening habits remain firmly rooted inside native music platforms.
Despite the rapid rise of autonomous background assistants across personal finance and productivity apps, Söderström emphasized that consumers prefer direct control over their audio curation and playback environments.
The executive's comments highlight Spotify's strategy to integrate proprietary AI features – such as its AI DJ, Prompted Playlists, and internal agent integrations – directly within its existing ecosystem rather than outsourcing discovery to external bots.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Redington Gulf, a subsidiary of technology distributor Redington Ltd, has signed a strategic collaboration agreement with Amazon Web Services (AWS) to drive cloud and artificial intelligence adoption across the Middle East, Turkey, and Africa (META) region.
Under the multi-year partnership, Redington Gulf will leverage AWS infrastructure and AI capabilities to help enterprise clients and small-to-medium businesses deploy and scale generative AI tools, cloud migration strategies, and advanced analytics.
The deal positions both companies to capture accelerating demand for cloud-native AI infrastructure across rapidly expanding digital markets in the META region.
Reuters contributed to this report.
EBay is eliminating roughly 1,000 positions – about 9% of its workforce – in its second major wave of job cuts this year as it pivots resources toward high-growth categories.
The reductions were outlined in an internal memo from CEO Jamie Iannone on Wednesday and confirmed by an eBay spokesperson.
"Our strategy is working," Iannone said. "We must decide where to direct our investments and resources to capitalize on future opportunities."
The San Jose-based e-commerce platform previously cut 800 roles (about 6% of staff) in February.
The new round of layoffs comes as eBay doubles down on luxury goods, collectibles , refurbished items, and secondhand fashion – bolstered by its $1.4 billion acquisition of Depop from Etsy in July – ahead of its third-quarter earnings report next week.
EBay deploys AI tools to help sellers expedite posting of goods on its platform.
This is a summary of FOX Business' Bradford Betz report.
Walmart announced a suite of new tools designed to allow autonomous AI agents to search products and make purchases on behalf of shoppers.
The move signals a major push into agentic e-commerce, drawing a sharp contrast with competitor Amazon, which has actively restricted third-party AI shopping bots from accessing its platform.
"The momentum and buy-in from top management teams seems to be making this into a real thing," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger said.
Under the new system, Walmart is introducing "Agent Profiles," allowing customers to set spending limits, monitor purchases separately, or require explicit approval for each transaction.
Additionally, the retailer launched the "Walmart Agent Gateway," enabling major AI platforms like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Meta’s Muse to connect directly to Walmart and Sam’s Club systems.
Available to all account holders without requiring a Walmart+ membership, the tools restrict AI agents from directly accessing sensitive payment card data while granting Walmart the authority to block any bots violating safety rules.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents accessing customer accounts, with some bots attempting actions independent of user commands, according to an Axios report Thursday.
Banks including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and others are racing to contain agent risks.
AT&T customers will decide whether AI agents can manage their accounts, CEO John Stankey said Wednesday , responding to Meta’s new Muse Spark AI model

articles.title_orig: A Typography Geek Pointed Out Something About The Space Shuttle Discovery And Now I Can't Unsee It
articles.title_zh: A Typography Geek Pointed Out Something About The Space Shuttle Discovery And Now I Can't Unsee It
articles.content_orig:
Even though I was born in the Apollo Era, barely, the spacecraft that I think had the most influence on my childhood had to be the Space Shuttles. I remember poring over diagrams and drawings of the shuttles in National Geographic foldouts, where they even took my attention from the Forbidden Nipples seen on some of the other pages. I remember watching that first launch of the shuttle Colombia in 1981, I remember the tragedy of the Challenger in 1986, and I remember covering the process of moving the orbiter Endeavour through the streets of Los Angeles to its eventual home at the California Science Center. And more recently, I’ve taken my kid to see the orbiter Discovery at the Udvar-Hazy Center just outside of Washington, DC.
It’s that orbiter that I want to talk about specifically, because I saw a social media post about the orbiter Discovery that grabbed my attention and held it with the sort of fierce grip I imagine Miss Piggy employs on Kermit’s impossibly thin limbs when they’re alone.
That post was on Threads, and I just figured out how to embed a post from that site, so here, you can see it for yourself:
Wait, what? Discovery has an upside-down ‘s’ in its name? How the hell did that happen? Discovery was usually considered, by astronauts and NASA people, the jewel in the Space Shuttle crown. It was recognized to be the most reliable and best-performing of all the orbiters, and had the most missions and time in space . Since it was first launched in 1984, Discovery completed 39 missions, spent in total a full year in space, and traveled 150 million miles.
The thing flew for 27 years, and somehow nobody noticed that the ‘s’ was upside down on the starboard side name text?
I mean, I guess I should be more understanding; I’ve seen it several times and never noticed, and it wasn’t until just tonight that I looked back at some old photos I took of Discovery the last time I was there and saw, holy crap, the dude on Threads was right. That ‘s’ is rotated 180°.
Now, the typography on the shuttle orbiters follows NASA’s carefully-planned and strictly-enforced graphic and typographic guidelines , which state that the typography used on the spacecraft should be Helvetica Medium:
Okay, let’s take a look at the typography on the orbiter:
(the ‘r’ on the font I used there feels a bit different, too, but this gets the point across and I have to get on a flight in a few hours so I’m gonna let that slide)
It’s a subtle difference, but as you can see, the starboard side’s name definitely has that flipped ‘s.’ It’s subtle, but the Helvetica ‘s’ is slightly wider on the bottom, giving the letter a somewhat more settled appearance. Here, look:
You can see the difference there, right? I feel like once it’s pointed out, you can’t help but notice it. The ‘v’ on the port side looks oddly thick, too, now that I’m looking at it.
I’ve been told that the graphics on these orbiters was applied using large stencils and special space-grade paint, and I’m sure the complex curves of the fuselage didn’t make the application of these elements easy. It’s understandable that a letter stencil may have been flipped around, but I am sort of surprised it was never corrected in its 27 years of service life.
All the other graphics and typography are applied with impressive precision; maybe there were people who knew that ‘s’ was wrong, but kind of liked that subtle imperfection, as it does add character to the spacecraft. I get that, absolutely. If I was in charge, I’d have just let it ride, too.
I still can’t believe I’d never clocked this before; as a typographic geek and a space geek who has spent far too much time looking at pictures of spacecraft in books and online, you’d think I’d have encountered this before, but, nope. Or if I did, it didn’t make enough of an impression to consciously note it or remember.
But now that it’s there? I can’t unsee it. And I’m sort of delighted by that.
Kerning around the v looks a little tight on the port side
Good type design is such a lost art… probably because it’s a tremendous ass-pain.
The closest most of use ever get is drawing the cool S in like 6th grade, then trying to write literally any word in that style and realizing it doesn’t work.

It showed for me but half off the screen like they usually do.  Meta won’t let me click any links since they want me to install the app and log in.
My first job out of college was with an aerospace company and we made some Shuttle parts.   Fantastic way to start out and still the most technically demanding job I’ve had.
Dude. I wonder if this was a deliberate move by a fellow Sid to sneak his name in upside-down and backwards on a space shuttle. If so, much respect.
This is now my favorite Shuttle Discovery fact. Those human touches on one of our greatest space-faring achievements really make it feel more humble. Kind of like how the letters just look spray painted on in general. Love that old space-based moving van.
Wow, that’s quite a discovery.
Jason kicking some NASA ‘s’.
If NASA was actually a real government organization, they would have got this right in the first place. Since it’s obvs Hollywood built – let’s just call it what it is: a simple continuity error.

My first read was exactly the same.

Wow. As a 25 year veteran sign guy, I can’t believe I never caught that either. I’ve handled I don’t know how many sets of Gemini letters, and it’s plainly obvious there’s a right-side-up when you’re holding the letter in your hand. I guess the odd curvature of the ship right there disguises it.
And now that I look more closely, that panel break cutting through the letters at an angle bugs me, too.
This really proves NASA did it…
When looking from the tarmac, the top part is further up and at an angle. Has to be bigger to optically match the bottom part that we’re looking at at a sharper angle.
Michelangelo’s David of fuselage ornamentation.

The only hole in your theory is that the ‘s’ is not flipped on the port side where it is farther up on sloped area near the windscreen.
Don’t touch it, it was the good luck charm for the ship.

I’m guessing the reason most of us don’t notice is the angle at which we see it combining with the curve of the craft. It’s a subtle enough issue that those things absolutely mask the problem.
But now that you’ve mentioned it, I will never unsee it.
In space, nobody can hear you scream about typography errors.

As European officials flag more trade restrictions, Beijing bristles at the idea it can be pushed into yielding to Brussels’ demands
In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.
Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris.
It has resulted in an awkward, terse trade peace: an agreement that was supposed to defuse a trade war has led to both sides, rhetorically at least, hardening their positions. With verbal volleys flying back and forth, doubts are already surfacing over whether this delicate ceasefire can hold until the next round of negotiations in January.

American Express is bringing Airbnb into its travel rewards platform.
The companies on Thursday announced a new partnership to bring more than 1 million Airbnb listings to Amex's travel portal and allow cardholders to earn rewards when booking the stays. It does not currently allow members to redeem points to pay for Airbnb bookings.
The launch adds Airbnb rentals to Amex's hotel portfolio, which includes more than 3,400 properties across its Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection programs.
Amex members with either the consumer or business Platinum card can also now apply their $600 annual lodging credit — previously called the hotel credit — to Airbnb's higher-end Luxe stays and take advantage of a new $250 statement credit on eligible Airbnb Experiences after making a Luxe booking.
"We're excited to bring more choice and flexibility to American Express Card Members with this exclusive partnership. Both of our companies exist to help people travel more and better, and this partnership helps people see more of the world by making travel more rewarding," said Juan David Borrero, head of partnerships at Airbnb, in a news release.
Membership points vary by card:
The changes come as competition among premium credit cards continues to ramp up.
Last year, American Express raised the annual fee on its premium Platinum card to $895. In turn, it's been investing in cardholder perks such as new lounges in airports and at big-ticket events and experiences as a way to attract more high-paying customers.
Earlier this month, it announced an expansion of its Centurion Lounges , with renovations coming to four existing lounges and new ones planned for Newark Liberty International Airport and London Heathrow Airport. The Newark lounge will be the largest in its network.
The partnership also comes as Americans continue to opt for travel and luxury experiences, even as prices for airfare, gas and hotels rise. Despite higher costs, more than half of Americans reported making no changes to their travel plans this summer , a recent study by travel insurance company Squaremouth found.

articles.title_zh: Horrifying video shows Mexican teen falling to her death from carnival ride
articles.content_orig:
A Mexican teenager died after falling from a carnival ride, with horrific video showing her flying out of her seat as the ride reached full speed.
Gabriela Rodriguez Tezoco, 18, died on Tuesday night following the accident at a festival in Los Cabos, Baja California Sur, local outlet Expreso reported .
Cell phone footage taken by another rider shows Tezoco plummeting to the ground from “The Pendulum,” a spinning ride at the Cabo San Lucas Traditional Festivals.
Other riders could be heard screaming as the teenager fell off while the ride kept spinning at high speed.
Emergency services rushed to treat Tezoco, who was taken to a nearby hospital, where she sadly died from her injuries early Wednesday morning.
“It is with deep sorrow that we report that the young woman who was injured in the incident that occurred in the amusement park area of ​​the Cabo San Lucas Traditional Festivals, and who was immediately transferred to receive medical attention, lost her life despite the efforts of the health personnel,” the Los Cabos City Council wrote on social media.
“The Pendulum” ride was closed in the wake of the incident while safety tests are carried out on it and the other attractions at the fair, Los Cabos mayor Christian Agundez told local reporters.
“Today, with the same spirit with which we come together to celebrate, we must come together to support Gabriela’s family. It could have been any one of us. You are not alone,” Agundez said during an appearance at a concert which was part of the festival.
An investigation has been opened both into the circumstances and to determine potential liability, the Baja California Sur State Attorney General’s Office reported on Wednesday.
So far, no arrests have been made, and no one responsible for the ride’s operation has been publicly identified.
Tezoco had just graduated this summer from the Baja California Sur College of Baccalaureate Studies.
“May your smile remain alive in our memory and may your memory always be a light that guides us,” the school said in a tribute.

articles.title_zh: What's behind Hamas's threat, and can it strike Israel? ‘The capabilities are there’
articles.content_orig:
Hamas officials reportedly delivered the message last week during a meeting at the Gaza office of UN humanitarian coordinator, asking him to convey it to Israeli authorities
Hamas has warned Israel that it is prepared to carry out another attack similar to the October 7, 2023, assault wherever an opportunity arises, according to a Ynet report.
The reported threat extended to attacks inside Israel, in the West Bank and abroad. Hamas officials reportedly delivered the message last week during a meeting at the Gaza office of UN humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov, asking him to convey it to Israeli authorities.
According to Ynet, Alakbarov passed the warning to Maj. Gen. Yoram Halevy, the coordinator of government activities in the territories, during a meeting on Wednesday. A document outlining the threats was then urgently circulated to senior political and security officials.
Israeli officials reportedly described the warning as unusually explicit and severe.
During their meeting with Alakbarov, Hamas officials reportedly complained about developments they said were weakening the group’s hold on Gaza.
These included continued Israeli military operations, changes to the “yellow line” marking IDF positions, and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas’s cancellation of elections scheduled for November 28.
According to Ynet’s account, the Hamas representatives said they were no longer willing to accept the current situation.
The warning comes as Israeli forces continue to target Hamas operatives in Gaza, including commanders and members of the group’s Nukhba unit.
Meanwhile, the Peace Council and international mediators are pressing Hamas to surrender its weapons. Israeli assessments cited by Ynet suggest the group is seeking to draw out negotiations without committing to disarmament.
Israel, for its part, has refused to allow a proposed technocratic governing committee or a Palestinian police force into Gaza, leaving arrangements for the territory’s administration and security unresolved.

articles.title_orig: Global Rush to Fix Security Flaw Uncovered by A.I. Leaves Sites Offline
articles.title_zh: Global Rush to Fix Security Flaw Uncovered by A.I. Leaves Sites Offline
articles.content_orig:
Governments and companies around the world are racing to fix vulnerabilities revealed by artificial intelligence that could affect 70% of the world’s websites.
Some websites and services briefly went dark after the set of vulnerabilities were announced Wednesday.
The US National Security Agenc y and Europe’s cybersecurity agency advised companies to take immediate action to address two critical flaws in PHP, a programming language that powers 70% of the world’s websites.
The flaws in PHP were uncovered and addressed by teams at OpenAI , Google-owned cybersecurity company Wiz, and another cybersecurity company, Calif . The underlying flaws had existed for a decade, but exploiting them involved a complex set of steps “at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” according to Wiz. Researchers then deployed AI to adapt techniques for taking advantage of those vulnerabilities – known as as “exploits” in cybersecurity – and analyze the results.
The bugs, collectively called PHP2Shell, could allow attackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords.
The PHP Foundation, the organization behind the coding language, has released a patch for the bugs, which have been hidden in their software for years, and is urging website operators to update their systems immediately. The CEO of Cloudflare said on X that his company’s network has observed millions of attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities in the past couple of days.
“With PHP behind such a vast share of the web, the exposure could reach almost everywhere people spend money online,” said Nigel Green, the CEO of deVere Group, a financial advisory firm.
“Booking platforms, marketplaces, subscription services, ticketing sites, delivery apps and utility portals could all be holding card details on systems built with the same kind of code,” he added.
The vulnerabilities involve an issue with how the PHP language works with a computer’s memory. When a website request unexpectedly ends, PHP could leave data behind in the memory that can be accessed and potentially corrupted or exposed later.
The bugs were discovered in late August but were disclosed to the public only on Wednesday, after PHP had come up with a fix.
AI played a crucial role in identifying and fixing vulnerabilities “that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade,” according to Wiz. The company called PHP the “backbone of the web” and said the episode marks an AI inflection point.
“What AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses,” Wiz researchers wrote in a blog post Wednesday, and then quickly exploit those weaknesses into a way to attack.
“With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work,” they added.
The flaws could allow attackers to remotely execute code, disrupt services and expose customer data, according to web infrastructure provider Cloudflare, which has been working with the PHP Foundation, Calif, OpenAI and Wiz to address the issue.
Researchers at Wiz used Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, Wiz Atlas and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol during the research process.
Global leaders urged organizations to take action. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that his cabinet was “closely monitoring the situation surrounding the vulnerabilities in PHP.”
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said companies should consider suspending services if necessary in order to reduce their exposure. “Please check if your publicly available websites use PHP, and prepare to apply the fix patch that will be released tonight… as soon as possible,” she posted on X Wednesday.
Japanese airline ANA, railway operator JR West and the country’s largest bank, MUFG, were among companies that reported some webpages and services temporarily suspended.
In Europe, government websites in France, Denmark, Finland and the Netherlands, including the Dutch cyber security agency, were temporarily taken offline while security fixes were implemented.
The Wikimedia Foundation, the non-profit that operates Wikipedia, told CNN Thursday that it was “in the process of addressing security vulnerabilities in PHP,” and that a number of its systems had been taken down as a “precautionary measure.”
Nearly three dozen UK government services are unavailable and four are “partially unavailable” while security upgrades take place, UK government minister Elizabeth Lloyd told the House of Lords Thursday. The Journal, Ireland’s second most-popular news outlet, was temporarily offline Thursday morning while it bolstered its “defences,” it said in a notice.
Wiz researchers say the issue is on par with the Heartbleed bug from 2014, which impacted an encryption technology estimated to be used by some two-thirds of the Web. Heartbleed allowed cybercriminals to access data that should have been protected.
Like Heartbleed, the researchers at Wiz say PHP2Shell could similarly serve as a turning point in cybersecurity. While the vulnerabilities existed for years, AI made it practical to deploy them.
“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” the researchers said.
“Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
– CNN’s John Liu, Anna Cooban, Amy Croffey and James Frater contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers disrupt key services and derail AI research
articles.title_zh: Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers disrupt key services and derail AI research
articles.content_orig:
From accessing their money to ordering a taxi or takeout, millions of Russians were feeling the impact of Ukrainian strikes on the data centers of the country’s internet giant Yandex in their daily life.
“I ended up in a situation where I had absolutely no money. Well, I had the money, but it was inaccessible,” said Irina, a blogger from St. Petersburg, who had not been able to access her money for four days when she spoke with NBC News last week.
Irina, who like several other people did not want her last name shared while she was speaking with a foreign news organization about a sensitive matter, said her rent was due the day the first outages happened, when she hoped “that it would be fixed in a few hours.” Days later, she still had no access to money to pay for utilities or even food for her small child.
The strikes that took place over several days this month were the first publicized attacks on Russian data centers as Ukraine seeks to bring the war home for Russians .
The disruption hit myriad services provided by Yandex, a tech giant akin to Google whose services are deeply integrated into daily life in Russia and whose digital infrastructure other third-party platforms rely on.
Many people took to social media to complain about not being able to order taxis or food delivery. Others reported not being able to access their files on the company’s storage service, while some even struggled to get into their homes after their digital keys went offline.
While most Yandex services have been coming back online, three people told NBC News they had been left locked out of their disposable cash and savings for days after disruptions to Yandex Pay, a digital payment service that many Russians use.
Irina, 21, said that in the future she will diversify her deposits across different banks and have a “substantial cash reserve” just in case.
Yandex said Oct. 9 that no employees were hurt and that it is working to restore service.
“Data centers are the iron heart of Yandex,” the statement said. “Their operation is critical for services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”
Anastasiya Mityaeva, 25, who splits her time between Moscow and the southern city of Krasnodar, said she was “shocked” by the outages, which initially left her family worried about being able to pay down their mortgage after her account, her mother’s account and her grandmother’s account were all inaccessible.
“The uncertainty was scary,” said Mityaeva, who has 2 million followers on TikTok and is originally from Russian-annexed Crimea. “We realized just how much hangs on Yandex. We did not quite appreciate it before.”
Mityaeva, who regained access to her money after several days, also had issues calling a taxi on the first day of the outages and encountered problems with the system to enter her apartment building. Her Yandex home voice assistant, equivalent to an Amazon Echo, stopped responding to requests to play music and turn off the lights.
She did not blame the company, saying Yandex was a “hostage of the situation,” adding: “I understand that this was not up to them. This came from the outside.”
Others were more critical of the company. Viktoria, 30, a barista from Moscow, said she plans to stop using Yandex completely after she was unable to access her money during the outages, describing it as the last straw after other recent issues.
She said Saturday that she once again had access to her money through Yandex Pay but that the service was displaying the wrong balance on her account.
Three taxi drivers in Moscow, who use Yandex’s taxi application to take orders and get paid, all told NBC News they could not see how much money they were making and could not withdraw their earnings during the outage. One of the drivers said he has stopped working altogether until the problem gets fixed. He is originally from Kyrgyzstan and did not know why the outages were happening.
Another driver, Valery from Krasnodar, had been on the job for only a few months, having previously worked at a packing center for Wildberries, Russia’s retail giant, whose warehouse was attacked by Ukrainian drones in July .
When the Yandex outages started, he said, the taxi app would show error messages or even send several cars for the same customer.
While that has been largely resolved, said Valery, 24, the biggest issue for him was that he could not withdraw the money that he had already earned with Yandex. “If I can’t access my pay in another week or two, I will start looking for another job,” he said.
In addition to Yandex, the data centers of Russia’s biggest bank, Sberbank, and the tech giant VK have also been targeted in recent days.
The chaos is no accident, analysts say. “Ukraine’s campaign from the start has had as one of its objectives bringing home to ordinary Russians the fact that they are at war and this involves consequences,” Keir Giles, an associate fellow at Chatham House, a British think tank, told NBC News.
The aim, Giles said, is for everyday Russians to conclude that their lives are being disrupted because of their leaders’ actions in waging war.
Yandex may also be a target because of its role in shaping what Russians see online, said Robert Tollast, a drone expert and researcher at the Royal United Services Institute in London.
Data centers also have growing military value, Tollast said, as both sides use battlefield data to improve operations and commanders’ situational awareness, potentially with AI-assisted planning.
Asked about the outages and whether the government was looking into financially assisting those affected, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was premature to talk about government support, because Yandex is “facing difficulties,” but it is “strong and powerful.” Meanwhile, Russian authorities were looking at protecting data centers after the “unprecedented attack,” Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said.
On Wednesday, President Vladimir Putin held a meeting on enhancing the level of digital security in Russia, but Peskov said it was not linked to the attacks on data centers.
Russia has increasingly ramped up its own attacks on Ukrainian data centers, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accusing Moscow of trying to “leave Ukrainians without the internet.” Ukraine was reciprocating those strikes by hitting Yandex, he said in a speech last week, adding without providing evidence that “it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms” because there were fewer Russian bots around. NBC News could not verify whether Yandex services’ going down had that effect.
While both sides have hit data centers, Russia’s were easier targets, said Mykhailo Samus, a Ukrainian military analyst and director of the New Geopolitics Research Network.
While Ukraine’s data centers are widely dispersed, many of Russia’s are concentrated in a handful of large facilities, he said, meaning a strike on a single site can disrupt services spanning transportation, internet access and payments.
“Very easy and very important,” he said.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Youth-Led Protests Sweep Across Europe
articles.title_zh: Youth-Led Protests Sweep Across Europe
articles.content_orig:
Fox News and others have toed president’s line – seemingly hoping unrest abroad will make people vote Republican
Donald Trump sought to capitalize on the scenes of unrest in France, telling a crowd in Kansas on Monday that “migrants” and “communists” were responsible, and that the scenes were “what the radical ‘Dumocrats’ want to do to America”.
As Republicans struggle to convince voters across the country ahead of November’s midterm elections, Trump’s allies in the conservative media have followed suit, seemingly hoping that the scenes in France can scare people to the polls.
Sean Hannity, perhaps Fox News’ most prominent host, delivered his version of the message on Tuesday. Speaking over clips of fires in France, with the chyron “A warning from Europe” emblazoned on the screen, Hannity said : “This is, sadly I argue, by design – an attempt by the left to destroy the free world, western civilisation, if you will.”
He added: “This is a preview of coming attractions here in America.”
Hannity wasn’t alone. On Monday, Fox News host Laura Ingraham had on Jamie Metzl, who describes himself as a “technology and healthcare futurist [and] geopolitical expert”, to draw the same comparison.
“If you like what you’re seeing in France then you should support these DSA candidates who are essentially calling for the same thing here,” Metzl said .
He was only echoing something Ingraham herself had said a few days earlier , in front of a cartoon version of a police flashing light with the words “A warning to America”. The chyron, as she spoke, could not have had a clearer message. It said in all capitals: “Don’t let America become France.”
“America, this is a warning. From the immigration disaster there, to the fiscal mismanagement, the same promises: free college, government-funded healthcare, tax the rich, climate change, open borders – they’re all being sold here, and they were implemented, some of them, here by AOC, Bernie, El-Sayed,” she said.
Most of the rest of Fox News agreed. Jesse Watters played clips of protests of violence in France on Monday, announcing that the goal is “to replace communism with capitalism”.
“It’s already started to happen here,” Watters added .
Lawrence Jones was of the same mind on Tuesday, reading out a tweet from JD Vance in which the vice-president said of the situation in France: “I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country.”
Jones responded : “The vice-president is exactly right.” He then interviewed Ben Domenech, an editor at the Daily Wire, who also agreed with Vance. The scenes in France, Domenech warned, are “the consequences of becoming apologetic about their values, viewing nationalism as something which is a dirty word”.
Fox News wasn’t alone. On Newsmax on Monday, Bianca de la Garza was busy asking Rick Santorum , the former Republican senator, if the situation in France is a “wake-up call for America”.
Santorum said it was. “The people who are running as democratic socialists or really just any sort of mainstream Democrats if you will, leftists, they want to bring the economy and style of government of Europe to this country,” he said. That, Santorum said, would lead to violent protests in the US.
“The standard of living of the average European is far below the standard of living of Americans,” Santorum said, which would come as a surprise to the people who are paid to research such things .
The same day Greta Van Susteren had interviewed Tom Emmer , the Republican congressman from Minnesota, who trotted out the same line.
“Look, we’ve got the same example in this country that we better be watching what’s going on in France. We want everyone to come to this country and chase their American dream. We want them to come here legally. And we also, Greta, want them to come to be Americans. We celebrate culture in this country like no one else,” he said.
“If you don’t come to this country to be an American, what you’re seeing in Paris is what is going to happen. You cannot have a different country within your country,” Emmer continued.
One America News (OAN), arguably the most rightwing of the three channels, was not about to be left out.
On Monday, OAN invited Andrew Fox , whom it described as a “cultural expert”, on to the channel to discuss the protests. Fox, who has 433 followers on X, said: “If we pay attention to what’s happening in Paris we can see our near future, if we don’t really toughen up immigration policy and the integration of how those immigrants become one with the nation they’re joining.”
Rounding out the message was David Pollack, one of OAN’s hosts, who at least adjusted his message slightly by looping in Italy. He tweeted a video of protesters in Italy, adding: “Now it’s happening in Italy: import the third world, and this is what you get. The sad thing was, this was all by design. And the Marxists are coming for the United States next.”

Today, Google and Voltus announced an expanded agreement to build a 1-gigawatt (GW) virtual power plant across the PJM grid region, which serves 67 million people across 13 states and Washington, D.C.
Voltus aggregates flexible capacity from local businesses and homes — like smart thermostats, batteries, and industrial assets — into a Google-funded virtual power plant. During peak demand, these assets temporarily reduce energy use to support grid reliability. In return, participating customers receive direct economic benefits, including bill savings and cash payments.
Building on a 100-megawatt agreement from earlier this year, this 10-fold expansion represents one of the largest known distributed capacity portfolios deployed by a hyperscaler to date.
This initiative reflects Google’s commitment to actively bring new capacity to local grids while strengthening regional reliability and affordability.
